comments.author: @drd4059
comments.text:
To be cynical, a narrow patent has advertising value to a marketing team.  A narrow patent has value to a company trying to raise capital from investors (who don't understand the difference between broad and narrow patents).  A narrow patent also has value imposing a cost on competitors doing a freedom to operate analysis.  Then there are pseudo patents based on the theme of rewording an undergraduate textbook into a patentese and claiming its original.  These probably would not survive a challenge, but my understanding is that the cost of invalidating an issued patent can cost $400K. The patent office prior art search is far from perfect.  My company is looking at pro-actively informing the patent office about prior art to knock out clones (in the same field as our patents) before they become issued and expensive to invalidate.  Your thoughts? 
Another topic of interest is omnibus patent applications which reduce initial cost by packing several related concepts into a very long specification.  The game with the examiner is to pack as much as possible into as few as possible issued patents.
